summary: A detector for CP-109 now exists, is proven to fail, and is run on nobody's behalf because package.json and .github/workflows/ci.yml are outside DB-015's grant (CP-112). This is the wiring request, and it is the same two-line job DB-014 handed over for its own detector. The reason to wire THIS one and not treat it as documentation is in `why_this_one`: the detector re-found, from the version numbers alone, the exact defect DB-014 found by execution the day before, and the class it covers has never had an instrument. It exits 0 today because all 53 findings are routed with a named owner, and it will exit nonzero the moment a new never-executed block appears that nobody has owned — which is the entire point of the disposition table being anchored to path:line.
why_this_one: Three reasons, in order of weight. (1) It is the only instrument in the repository that can see this class. CP-104 and CP-085 and CP-109 are all the same failure, and all three were found by hand, by one agent, at the cost of a full chain replay each time. (2) It is anchored so it cannot go quietly stale: a disposition that stops matching its block makes the check FAIL, so the day someone renumbers a migration the check asks a human rather than reporting clean. (3) Its false-negative direction is guarded, which is the direction that matters: there is no code path in the module that can emit the verdict `clean`, and the CLI refuses to report clean unless it has actually found the two instances CP-109 confirmed.

Neither is a regression in the chain's health and neither should be silenced by editing the disposition without looking.

completed: Generalized the DB-014 harness into a detector over every guard-guarded block in the chain, in version order, with the guard's OWN expression executed against a real catalog rather than parsed.

Found 53 never-executed blocks across 33 migrations, including 15 RLS-policy blocks over 8 tables, 4 `is null then return` guards that skip the rest of their block, 4 `drop policy`-only blocks, and 10 inert post-condition assertions in the chain's three newest migrations.
Routed every one of the 53 to a named owner with a severity, in 12 groups, mechanically enforced in both directions by assertDispositionsAreComplete().

Proved the detector can fail: 22 synthetic fixtures with expected verdicts, an order-mutation proof over the REAL chain that renumbers a migration and requires the finding to disappear, two negative controls in the harness on synthetic chains that differ only in order, and an exit-code assertion that an unrouted finding is nonzero.

Proved the detector cannot see its own target silently: assertAnchorsSeen() makes the CLI refuse to report clean unless it found both CP-109-confirmed instances, and a missing anchor is a failure rather than a pass.

Recorded five defects this detector had, each pinned by a fixture — three of them false positives in files whose names are security migrations, and one of them a clean report from an instrument that had found zero guard sites in the chain.

blockers: NONE for the wiring. The detector is implemented, tested, executed and routed. This handoff exists because CP-112 puts package.json and .github/workflows/ci.yml outside DB-015's grant, and expanding a grant unilaterally is the collision class CP-112 was written to prevent.

The detector's static path is a MODEL of execution, not execution. It is kept honest by the harness, which runs both and asserts no guard the static path calls live is called dead by the server — 0 contradictions over 446 executed sites on this run. The executed path itself over-reports by construction (one psql connection cannot hold two catalog states at once), so it is a cross-check and not a second finding set, and the report says so under `replay.caveat`.
